Unrelated question before that: what exactly is stalemate, and why is it a draw instead of a loss?

Stalemate happens when the side to move is not in check but has no legal move at all, and the game is then declared a draw. Before that, unrelated question: what is the touch move rule?

In tournament play, if you touch one of your own pieces on your turn, you must move it if it has a legal move. If you touch an opponent's piece, you must capture it if you can. If you deliberately let go of a piece on a square, that move is final, and you may adjust a piece without moving it by saying "j'adoube" or "I adjust" first.

En passant lets a pawn that has just advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn that is standing right beside it on the fifth rank, as if the advance had moved only one square. Unrelated question before that: what are the first moves of the Queen's Gambit?

The Queen's Gambit begins with 1.d4 d5 2.c4, offering a pawn on c4 to open lines for White's center. Black usually answers with ...e6 to keep the pawn on d5 supported, or with ...c6 in the Slav structure. After that, play often develops knights to c3 and f3 and bishops to g5 or f4.
Another unrelated one: how does a rook move?

A rook moves any number of empty squares along a rank or a file, horizontally or vertically. It cannot move diagonally, and it stops when it reaches a piece, capturing that piece if it belongs to the opponent. Castling is the one special case where a rook moves together with the king.

Unrelated question before we continue: what is a fork in chess?

A fork is a single move that attacks two or more enemy pieces at once, so the opponent can only save one of them. Knights are especially good at forking because their jumps reach squares other pieces can't easily attack. Pawns, queens and kings can also fork, though a king fork is usually called something else in practice.
Thanks. Now how exactly does a rook move?

A rook moves any number of squares along a rank or a file, horizontally or vertically, as long as no piece is in the way. It captures by landing on an enemy piece it can reach along those lines. Rooks are strongest on open files and ranks.

Stalemate happens when the side to move is not in check but has no legal move at all. A fianchetto is a development plan where a bishop is placed on the long diagonal after the pawn in front of it advances two squares. For White, the typical version is g3 followed by Bg2, with the bishop aimed down the long diagonal toward the enemy king on the other side. Unrelated question before the puzzle: what exactly is a pin in chess?

A pin is when a piece is attacked and cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it to capture. The classic example is a bishop on g5 pinning a knight on f6 against a queen on d8, since moving the knight would let the bishop take the queen. Absolute pins involve the king itself, which makes the pinned piece unable to move at all.

Unrelated question, before I move: what's Fool's Mate in general, how does it work?

Fool's Mate is the fastest possible checkmate in chess, played after just two moves by each side in the opening. White plays f3 and g4, weakening the king's diagonal, then Black plays queen to h4 giving check along the diagonal to the white king on e1. The king has no escape because the pawns on f3 and g4 block the squares it would need, so it is checkmate.

Different topic: what is a fianchetto?

A fianchetto is developing a bishop by moving the adjacent knight's pawn one or two squares, then placing the bishop on the long diagonal behind it. The bishop on g2 or b2 for White, or g7 or b7 for Black, becomes a powerful long-range piece aimed at the center. Kings often castle on that side to be sheltered by the fianchettoed bishop.

unrelated question before that: what is a fianchetto?

A fianchetto is developing a bishop to the long diagonal by first moving the adjacent knight's pawn one or two squares, so the bishop fits on the g2 or b2 square (for white) or g7 or b7 (for black). The bishop then sits behind the pawn and eyes the long diagonal toward the enemy king. It's a common opening setup in the King's Indian and Catalan.

Threefold repetition is a draw claim that applies when the same position, with the same side to move, has occurred three times, not necessarily consecutively. Unrelated question before the next one: what is a skewer in chess?

A skewer is an attack on two pieces lined up on the same line, where the front piece is more valuable and must move out of the way, exposing the piece behind it to capture. En passant lets a pawn that has just advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn that stands beside it on the adjacent file, as if the advance had moved only one square. Unrelated question before that: what is a pin in chess?

A pin is when a piece is stopped from moving because doing so would expose a more valuable piece behind it to capture, usually the king. Absolute pins are against the king itself and are illegal to break; relative pins against other pieces are allowed but cost material if you ignore them. Pins are often used to restrict a defender's options and set up a winning attack.
Before that, how does en passant work?

En passant lets a pawn that has advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn that could have captured it had it moved only one square. The capture must happen immediately on the next move, and the capturing pawn lands on the square the passed pawn skipped over. It is the only capture in chess where the target square is not the square the captured piece occupies.

Unrelated question, before that: what is Fool's Mate, exactly? I remember hearing about it as a kid.

Fool's Mate is the fastest checkmate possible in chess, done in just two moves by each side, with White playing f3 and then g4, and Black replying e5 and then Qh4 mate. The idea is that White weakens the king's diagonal and shelter, and Black's queen slides to h4 to give checkmate along that open diagonal to the king on e1. It only works when the opponent blunders badly, so it is mostly a warning about not opening your king's cover too early.

The world champion before Bobby Fischer was Tigran Petrosian, who held the title from 1963 to 1969. He was known for a very solid, defensive style that made it hard for opponents to create chances.

Unrelated question, before that: how does castling work, and where do the king and rook end up?

Castling is a king move in which the king moves two squares toward a rook, and the rook jumps over to the square the king crossed. Kingside castling puts the king on g1 and the rook on f1 for White, and queenside castling puts the king on c1 and the rook on d1. You can only castle if neither piece has moved, the squares between them are empty, the king is not in check, and it does not pass through or land on an attacked square.

Before that, what is a pin in chess?

A pin is when a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it to capture, most often a piece pinned against the king. A absolute pin means the pinned piece cannot legally move at all, while a relative pin means moving it would lose material rather than being illegal. Pins are useful for restricting an opponent's pieces and for winning material.

Unrelated question before that: what is a fianchetto?

A fianchetto is developing a bishop to the long diagonal by moving the adjacent knight's pawn one or two squares forward first, typically on the kingside or queenside with the b-pawn or g-pawn. The bishop then sits on b2 or g2 for White, or b7 or g7 for Black, aiming down the long diagonal toward the opposing king. It is a common opening setup that strengthens control of the center.

Unrelated question before that: what does threefold repetition mean, and how is it claimed?

Threefold repetition is a draw that can be claimed when the same position, with the same side to move and the same available castling and en passant rights, has occurred three times, not necessarily consecutively. A player claims it with the arbiter or, in many online settings, by pressing the claim button on their turn. The game is drawn only if the claim is made, since it is not automatic.

A knight on d4 attacks b3, b5, c2, c6, e2, e6, f3 and f5. Those are its eight jumps, two squares in one direction and one square perpendicular.

The London System usually begins with 1. d4 followed by 2. Bf4, then 3. e3, 4. Nf3, 5. Bd3, 6. c3 and 7. Nbd2, building a solid setup. Black's common replies include ...d5 and ...Nf6, and the system is popular because it needs little memorization.

Unrelated question before that: how does en passant work?

En passant lets a pawn that has just advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn that stands beside it on the fifth rank, as if the pawn had moved only one square. The Queen's Gambit begins with White playing pawn to queen four, and Black usually answers with pawn to queen four as well. White then offers a gambit with pawn to queen's bishop four, inviting Black to accept or decline it. Common follow-ups for White are knight to queen's bishop three and bishop to the g5 square to develop.

Before we continue, unrelated question: what exactly is a pin in chess, and how does it differ from a skewer?

A pin is a situation where a piece is attacked and cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it on the same line, usually the king. The two are mirror images: a pin restricts the front piece, while a skewer forces the front piece to give way.

Before that, unrelated question: how does a rook move on the board?

A rook moves any number of empty squares in a straight line, either along a rank (a horizontal row) or along a file (a vertical column). Unrelated question before that: what is a pin in chess?

A pin is when a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it to capture. For example, a bishop that attacks a knight with a king behind it on the same diagonal pins the knight, because moving the knight would expose the king to check. Unrelated question, before we return to this. What does zugzwang mean in chess?

Zugzwang is a position in which the player to move would prefer to pass, because every legal move they have worsens their position. It arises most often in endgames, where having the move is itself a disadvantage. The concept is about forced concessions, not about any single piece or square.

A rook moves any number of unoccupied squares along a rank or a file, in a straight line. It cannot move diagonally, and it stops when it reaches a piece, capturing it if that piece belongs to the opponent. It may also take part in castling with the king under the usual conditions.

unrelated question before that: in the Ruy Lopez, what are the first few moves and why does white play the bishop to b5?

The Ruy Lopez begins with 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5, pinning the knight on c6 against the black king's support and preparing to attack the pawn structure. A fianchetto is developing a bishop to the second or seventh rank by first moving the adjacent knight's pawn one or two squares, so the bishop sits on a long diagonal behind it. Unrelated question before we continue: what is a fork in chess? Give me a precise explanation with an example.

A fork is a single move that attacks two or more enemy pieces at once, so the opponent can only save one of them. Unrelated question before that: how does en passant work?

En passant lets a pawn that has just advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn that stands beside it on the fifth rank, as if the pawn had only moved one square. The capture must be made immediately on the very next turn, and the capturing pawn moves diagonally onto the square the passed pawn skipped over, removing the passed pawn from the board. It is only possible on the turn right after the two-square advance; if the chance is not taken then, it is lost.

Unrelated question first: what exactly is a discovered check?

A discovered check happens when a piece moves out of the line between a friendly sliding piece (a rook, bishop, or queen) and the enemy king, so that the sliding piece now attacks the king. The moving piece can then make any move it likes, including a second threat, while the check is already on the board. Because the check comes from the piece that was behind, the opponent must answer it before anything else.
Before that, which bishop is the light-squared bishop at the start of a game?

The light-squared bishop is the one that starts on a light square, which for White is the one placed between the knight and the queen's side of the board. Each side has one light-squared and one dark-squared bishop, and they can never change square color because bishops only move diagonally.

A skewer is an attack on two pieces lined up along a line, where the front piece is more valuable and must move out of the way, exposing the piece behind it to capture. Zugzwang is a position where the side to move is forced to make a damaging move because every legal move worsens its position, even though passing would have been better. It is common in endgames with few pawns and pieces, where the obligation to move is what decides the game.

unrelated question before that, how does castling work exactly? where do the king and rook end up?

Castling moves your king two squares toward a rook along the back rank, and that rook jumps over the king to the square right next to it. Kingside castling puts the king on the g-file and the rook on the f-file, while queenside castling puts the king on the c-file and the rook on the d-file. You can only castle if neither piece has moved, the squares between them are empty, the king is not in check, and it does not pass through or land on an attacked square.

A fianchetto is a development setup where a bishop is placed on the long diagonal after the knight's pawn is moved one or two squares forward, so the bishop sits behind it. En passant lets a pawn that has advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn that stands beside it on the same rank, as if it had moved only one square. Stalemate occurs when the side to move is not in check but has no legal move at all, so the game is ended as a draw. The rule exists so that a player who is clearly winning cannot be left unable to move without losing the game. Any position where the side to move has no legal moves and is not in check is stalemate, regardless of the material on the board.

Scholar's Mate is a four-move trap that uses the queen and the bishop together. White plays e4, then Bc4, then Qh5, then Qxf7#. The queen takes the f7 pawn, which is protected only by the king, and the bishop on c4 covers that square so the king cannot recapture.

unrelated question before that, how does en passant work exactly

En passant lets a pawn that has just advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn standing beside it on the same rank, as if that pawn had only moved one square. The capture must happen immediately on the very next move, and the capturing pawn lands diagonally behind the advanced pawn, which is removed from the board. It is only legal in response to that double step, never later.

Unrelated question before we continue: what does zugzwang mean in chess?

Zugzwang is a position where the side to move is forced to make a move that worsens its situation, because every legal move is bad. It often happens in endgames where having to move, rather than being able to pass, decides the game. Pawn structures and king opposition are common places where it appears.

A pin is when a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it to capture. For example, a bishop might pin a knight against a king on the same diagonal. The pinned piece is not technically lost, but moving it is illegal or very costly.

Unrelated question, before that: how does castling work in chess, and where do the king and rook end up?

Castling is a special king move in which the king moves two squares toward a rook, and the rook jumps over to the square the king crossed. Kingside castling puts the king on g1 and the rook on f1 for White, and queenside castling puts the king on c1 and the rook on d1.
